headline: High-risk shared-workspace pair: Cursor can auto-run shell/MCP actions while Copilot can propose edits, creating dangerous default paths for prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor ingests workspace files, clipboard, and MCP outputs, and can auto-run commands in Yolo mode; Copilot reads repo context/open buffers and proposes edits. The pair has a shared local-filesystem bridge, so attacker-controlled content in one tool can influence the other. This is not provably blocked by either profile.
conditions: IF Cursor is run in Yolo mode and consumes untrusted workspace content, THEN injected instructions can reach its tool loop.
IF Copilot Workspace or chat consumes Cursor-authored files without provenance checks, THEN malicious instructions can propagate.
mitigations: Disable Yolo mode for shared projects.
Keep untrusted content in a separate workspace.
Require human review of any generated patch before applying.
Use provenance comments or file headers for agent-authored content.
requires-engineering: add content provenance tagging between tools.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cursor touches clipboard contents, open files, and broad network egress to model providers and MCP servers; Copilot reads repo context and sends it to api.githubcopilot.com. In a shared workspace, sensitive code or notes can flow from either agent into vendor backends. The profiles do not show a hard isolation boundary, so leakage is plausible in default use.
conditions: IF sensitive files are present in the shared workspace, THEN both agents can ingest them.
IF Cursor MCP servers or model providers retain prompts, THEN copied context can leave the host.
IF Copilot is granted repo context on a sensitive repository, THEN that context is transmitted to GitHub services.
mitigations: Remove secrets from the shared workspace.
Restrict Cursor MCP servers to trusted endpoints only.
Use a separate repo clone for sensitive material.
Review Copilot repo access before enabling chat/workspace.
requires-engineering: enforce redaction before outbound model calls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Cursor can write the filesystem, modify git state, execute shell, and spawn subprocesses; Copilot can also write files and modify git state. They share state via the local filesystem or editor buffers, so concurrent edits and git mutations can collide by default. This creates a real risk of irreversible repo corruption or conflicting commits.
conditions: IF both agents edit the same branch or files concurrently, THEN git and filesystem conflicts can occur.
IF Cursor auto-runs shell commands while Copilot applies edits, THEN race conditions can corrupt the working tree.
mitigations: Use one agent at a time per branch.
Pause Copilot Workspace while Cursor is executing commands.
Commit or stash before switching agents.
Limit both agents to read-only review on critical branches.
requires-engineering: add file-level locking and merge arbitration.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Copilot Workspace plans and applies edits, while Cursor can generate and act on multi-step tool outputs. If one agent's output is treated as authoritative by the other, mistakes can cascade into code changes or shell actions without verification. The profiles show no mandatory cross-check, so the default interaction is unsafe.
conditions: IF Copilot applies edits derived from Cursor-generated text without review, THEN errors can be committed.
IF Cursor executes commands based on Copilot-produced patches or summaries, THEN incorrect assumptions can trigger downstream actions.
mitigations: Require a human to verify every patch before apply.
Use a second-pass reviewer for generated code.
Disable auto-apply features on both agents.
Keep action-taking tasks separate from drafting tasks.
requires-engineering: add verification gates between agent outputs and actions.

E_compliance.rationale: Cursor is documented as handling model provider API keys and broad network egress to third-party model providers and MCP servers, while Copilot sends repo context to GitHub services under a GitHub OAuth scope. For regulated code or secrets, this creates a compliance mismatch risk around residency, retention, and access control. The profiles do not show aligned retention or DPA guarantees.
conditions: IF regulated data or secrets are present in the workspace, THEN outbound processing may violate policy.
IF the repository is subject to strict retention or residency rules, THEN the two vendors' defaults may diverge.
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from the shared workspace.
Review vendor privacy and retention settings before use.
Use separate accounts for sensitive and non-sensitive repos.
Disable optional context sharing features.
requires-engineering: obtain and enforce a DPA/residency-approved deployment.
